books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, A. The Emergence of a National Culture

stimulus.text: In 1828 Noah Webster published An American Dictionary of the English Language. Webster gave American words American spellings: color for colour, center for centre, defense for defence, traveling for travelling. He wanted a dictionary that belonged to the United States, not to Britain.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.9 A: Webster sought to codify a specifically American dictionary, separate from British English, publishing his American Dictionary of the English Language in 1828. Spelling examples are Webster's standard American forms. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Webster's dictionary best illustrates which of the following developments?

options.text: The growth of factory towns along New England rivers
options.misconception: Mills and dictionaries both grew in the 1820s, so it is easy to tie any new book to the factories.

options.text: The growth of a distinct American national culture
The religious revivals of the Second Great Awakening
options.misconception: Revival preachers also published books, so it is easy to link Webster's work to religion.

options.text: The spread of slavery into the southwestern territories
options.misconception: Slavery spread in the same decades, so it is easy to attach any 1820s development to it.

rationales.A: The dictionary was about language and national identity, not about mill towns or factory work.
rationales.B: Webster deliberately made American English its own system, separate from British English.
rationales.C: Webster's project was about words and spelling, not about revival preaching or conversion.
rationales.D: The dictionary said nothing about slavery or where it spread; its subject was American English.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Webster actually did. He wrote a dictionary with American spellings.
2. Ask why that mattered. A nation that spells its own words is saying its language is its own.
Background: Barron's places Webster in the national culture that grew after the War of 1812.
Remember: a dictionary can be a declaration of independence, written one spelling at a time.
